overview: Here “Suebi” means the kingdom in northwestern Iberia, centred on Braga, rather than every ancient group that used the name elsewhere in Europe. Its rulers governed a landscape inherited from Roman Gallaecia. The imported 500 to 600 map layer is a broad territorial approximation and extends past the kingdom’s conquest in 585; it should not imply uninterrupted Suevic independence throughout that century.

periods.title: The later Suevic kingdom
periods.summary: Braga remained a royal and ecclesiastical centre.

periods.title: After the conquest
periods.summary: The final map years fall under Visigothic government.

items.text: Braga had already been the Roman city of Bracara Augusta before it became a centre of Suevic royal power. Church councils met there in 561 and 572. Political authority and the organisation of Christian communities therefore developed around an existing city, rather than a newly built royal camp.

At Dume near Braga, archaeology has exposed the Suevic basilica and monastery beneath the present parish church and surrounding spaces. The site also contains an older Roman bathing complex. Keeping those phases separate matters: finding a bath beside a monastery does not prove that sixth-century monks used it unchanged.

Suevic coins could retain the names of Roman emperors. Two gold tremisses described in the official Galician heritage inventory name Honorius and Valentinian; each weighs 1.35 grams. A kingdom could assert its own authority while using familiar imperial money designs. These tiny valuable coins were not evidence that every purchase used gold.

Imported fine tableware and amphoras found in Vigo reveal sustained trade with North Africa, southern Iberia, the eastern Mediterranean, Britain and western Gaul. The evidence spans the fourth to seventh centuries, including Suevic rule. Northwestern Iberia remained connected to distant producers even after Roman political control ended.

At the hilltop settlement of Viladonga, pottery research identifies intensive occupation in the fifth and early sixth centuries. Some grey-fired bowls and small dishes fit sixth-century styles. A change in rulers did not stop households from needing serving dishes, drinking vessels and reliable containers.

Viladonga’s late pottery also includes large handmade cooking dishes, roughly 24 to 34 centimetres across the mouth, with flat bottoms and thick walls. These practical vessels take us into food preparation, even when the remains do not identify the exact meal once cooked in each pot.

The Viladonga study counted 535 fragments of coated pottery, about twenty-two percent of its analysed late assemblage, linked to production around Lugo. Ordinary crockery travelled through regional markets as well as across seas. The figures describe this studied collection, not every pot used in the kingdom.

In a sermon intended for rural listeners, Martin of Braga recalled baptism as a conversation: a priest asked questions and the person answered, or a sponsor answered if the candidate could not. His account gives a glimpse of the people helping one another take part in a religious ceremony.

Martin complained about candles at stones, trees and springs, and about bread being thrown into a spring. These are practices he condemned, rather than a neutral survey of what everyone did. His irritation preserves details of religious disagreements that a list of kings would never mention.

The same sermon urged listeners to feed a hungry poor person and refresh a tired guest. Martin’s ideal of a good community involved practical hospitality as well as worship. The instruction tells us what he wanted people to do; it does not prove every traveller received a warm welcome.

sections.title: Advice to a ruler and words on stone

items.text: King Miro asked Martin for guidance on living and governing. The resulting Formula vitae honestae organised advice around four virtues and drew on classical moral thought. Later generations copied it widely across Europe. Royal education could include learning how to judge, restrain oneself and treat other people, alongside exercising power.

Martin’s Latin advice includes “De dubiis non definias”, meaning “Do not make firm judgments about doubtful things”. This wording comes from a modern transcription of his sixth-century work, not his original handwriting. It sounds like useful advice for checking a rumour before passing it on.

The Rocas inscription begins “[H]EREDITAS”, Latin for “inheritance” or “property”, and names people associated with a text dated to 573. The bracket marks a supplied letter. The museum cautions that the surviving stone may be a ninth- or tenth-century copy; it cannot securely be treated as the original sixth-century carving.

The Rocas text has often been called a monastery’s foundation record, but its wording may instead record an endowment or property arrangement. Even the last name-like group is uncertain. This small stone connects religious life with gifts, ownership and memory, while leaving the precise transaction open to debate.

ending.text: Visigothic forces conquered the kingdom in 585, and Braga became the centre of a Visigothic province. This ended Suevic royal independence before the imported map’s 600 endpoint. Towns, churches and households continued under changed government; the conquest date is not a date when all their inhabitants disappeared.
